subject: Medicine
summary: Obesity is excess white adipose tissue from chronic energy imbalance. In East Africa, infections, HIV, TB, and herbal remedies can precipitate or mask it. Management focuses on lifestyle, safe pharmacology, and monitoring for metabolic complications.

sections.p: Obesity is defined by a body mass index (BMI) ≥30 kg/m². In children, use age‑specific percentiles (≥95th). Waist circumference >102 cm in men or >88 cm in women indicates central obesity.

t.b: Is the patient overweight or obese? A BMI ≥30 kg/m² confirms obesity
Assesses visceral fat; >102 cm men, >88 cm women raises cardiovascular risk

sections.p: Classify by BMI: Class I (30–34.9), Class II (35–39.9), Class III (≥40). Central obesity adds risk irrespective of BMI.

t.b: Guides intensity of intervention; higher class needs more aggressive therapy

sections.p: In low‑resource settings, chronic infections (HIV, TB, malaria), parasitic helminths, and nutritional shifts (high‑calorie, low‑fiber diets) are common drivers. Herbal remedies may mask symptoms.
b: HIV infection – lipodystrophy and metabolic syndrome
TB – chronic inflammation and altered appetite
Malaria – intermittent fever and weight loss followed by rebound
Helminthic infections – malabsorption then compensatory overeating
High‑calorie diets – refined sugars, fried foods

t.b: Is HIV contributing to metabolic changes? Positive status warrants antiretroviral review
Rule out hepatitis B/C which can affect metabolism

sections.p: Patients may report fatigue, shortness of breath, joint pain, and sleep apnea. Physical exam shows central fat, reduced chest expansion, and possible acanthosis nigricans.

t.b: Detects reduced breath sounds indicating restrictive pattern

sections.p: Prioritize inexpensive tests; use clinical judgment when labs are unavailable.

t.b: Screen for diabetes; >126 mg/dL indicates diabetes
Assesses long‑term glycaemic control; >6.5 % suggests diabetes
Elevated triglycerides >150 mg/dL or LDL >130 mg/dL raise cardiovascular risk
Hypertension (>140/90 mmHg) is common in obesity

sections.p: Watch for acute complications: obstructive sleep apnoea, DVT, pulmonary embolism, type 2 diabetes, hypertension, fatty liver, and heart failure.

t.b: Elevated in suspected DVT/PE; if high, proceed to imaging

sections.p: Treat underlying causes first, then implement lifestyle and pharmacologic strategies tailored to resource limits.
b: Counselling on diet: reduce refined carbs, increase fruits/veg
Encourage physical activity: walking, community exercise
Pharmacology: metformin for pre‑diabetes/diabetes; statins for dyslipidaemia; avoid thiazolidinediones due to hepatotoxicity

t.b: Improves insulin sensitivity; avoid in renal impairment

sections.p: Regular monitoring of weight, BP, glucose, lipids, and liver enzymes every 3–6 months. Community education on healthy diets and physical activity is key.
Differential includes lipodystrophy, hypothyroidism, Cushing’s syndrome, and chronic infections causing weight gain.

t.b: Elevated in hypothyroidism; normal in obesity

sections.p: In low‑resource settings, BMI may be inaccurate if height is measured incorrectly; waist circumference can be over‑estimated if clothing is thick.

whenToSeekHelp: Acute shortness of breath, chest pain, sudden leg swelling, severe headache, visual changes

faq.q: Can obesity be diagnosed without a scale?
faq.a: Yes, use waist circumference and clinical assessment, but BMI is preferred when possible.

faq.q: What is the safest drug for weight loss in pregnancy?
faq.a: No pharmacologic agent is recommended; focus on nutrition and safe exercise.
Antiretroviral therapy can cause lipodystrophy and metabolic syndrome, leading to central fat accumulation.

exam: A 28‑year‑old woman with BMI 32 presents with fatigue and joint pain. What is the first investigation? — Fasting glucose to screen for diabetes.
A patient with obesity develops sudden leg swelling. What is the next step? — D‑dimer to rule out DVT, followed by ultrasound if positive.
Why is metformin preferred over sulphonylureas in obese patients with pre‑diabetes? — It improves insulin sensitivity and has weight‑neutral or weight‑loss effect.
A patient on antiretrovirals shows central obesity. Which complication should you screen for? — Dyslipidaemia and insulin resistance.
What lifestyle advice is most effective in low‑resource settings? — Increase daily walking and reduce refined carbohydrate intake.
Why should thiazolidinediones be avoided in obese patients with liver disease? — They can cause hepatotoxicity and fluid retention.
